subject: Workshop Thursday Oct 5th on Dat for data sharing, archiving, and syncing

messages.author: 38f9cffaa23acd56
messages.subject: Workshop Thursday Oct 5th on Dat for data sharing, archiving, and syncing
parts:
Hi DRUGgies,

Not strictly R-related, but thought it could be of use to many of you. We're hosting the team behind Dat, a tool that uses decentralized technology to enable fast and secure data archiving, sharing, and syncing, for a two hour workshop on using their tools. I'm personally interested in it because I think it will solve many issues we have managing, versioning, and sharing data. The workshop will be from 12pm-2pm on Thursday, October 5th (this week!) in the conference room at the Center for Watershed Sciences (map).

This workshop has space for *15* participants only and you can sign up here. You will receive a confirmation email sometime this coming week with information about if you have been accepted. Anyone is welcome, but Center for Watershed Sciences affiliates will get priority. If this workshop fills and there's enough interest, we'll try to put together another workshop in early 2018 when the Dat team is back on campus.

Please feel free to forward this to anyone you think would be interested. More information on workshop content, from the creators, is below:
--------

Code for Science & Society and the UC Curation Center (CDL UC3) will lead a beginner-friendly tutorial on Dat, a tool that uses decentralized technology to enable fast and secure data archiving, sharing, and syncing. Dat is inspired by the best parts of Git, BitTorrent, and Dropbox —  it's a tool designed for data. Come check it out, discuss the potential of decentralized computing in research, and talk to the Dat in the Lab project leads. The session will include a short introduction to Dat and the Dat in the Lab project, a tutorial where participants can practice using Dat hands-on, and time for discussion and questions with Stephen Abrams (CDL UC3), Max Odgen (Code for Science and Dat), and Danielle Robinson (Code for Science and Dat). You can learn more about how it all works by reviewing Dat's key concepts, or get more technical by reading the Dat whitepaper.

This session will be hands-on and participants should bring a laptop. We will use the command line, however no technical skills are required to attend the workshop — we love working with beginners. Our goal is to create a welcoming environment for people at all levels to have fun with decentralized technology and discuss the ways Dat could be used in their research workflows.


Nick Santos
UC Davis Center for Watershed Sciences
